item.title: The Student Loan Reset: How New Repayment Rules Are Changing Monthly Bills for Millions of Borrowers
item.body:
Federal student loan repayment is going through its biggest rewrite in years. Congress changed the rules in the 2025 budget reconciliation law, and the Department of Education is phasing those changes in. New repayment plans, new borrowing limits and a shrinking menu of income-driven options mean the amount many graduates owe each month may look different from what they planned.

This guide covers who is affected, what to check in your loan servicer account, and how the changes could flow through to household budgets and credit. It is general information, not financial or legal advice. Timelines and details can shift with new regulations and court rulings, so confirm specifics at StudentAid.gov or with your servicer.

## The big picture

Three shifts matter most:

1. **A new income-based plan.** The Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) is available to borrowers starting July 1, 2026.
2. **A smaller set of plans over time.** Several existing income-driven plans are being phased out.
3. **New borrowing caps.** Limits on how much students and parents can borrow apply to new loans made on or after July 1, 2026.

## The Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP)

RAP ties your monthly payment to your adjusted gross income (AGI) instead of a share of discretionary income. Based on the law's published structure:

- Payments range from roughly 1% to 10% of AGI, rising as income rises.
- There is a minimum monthly payment of $10.
- The payment is reduced by $50 per month for each dependent child.
- If your payment doesn't cover the monthly interest, the unpaid interest is waived. In addition, the plan matches principal reduction, up to $50 a month, when your payment is small.
- Remaining balances may be forgiven after 30 years of qualifying payments.

For many lower- and middle-income borrowers, RAP can produce a lower or more predictable bill than a standard schedule. Higher earners may pay more than they would under some older income-driven plans. Because the formula uses total AGI, it can behave differently from plans you may be used to. Use the official Loan Simulator rather than guessing.

## What happens to older plans

Plans that existed before the change are on different clocks:

- **SAVE.** This plan has been tied up in litigation and many enrolled borrowers were placed in forbearance. Under the new law it is being wound down. If you were in SAVE, watch for notices about choosing a new plan.
- **PAYE and ICR.** These are slated to close to new enrollment, and the law sets a deadline of July 1, 2028 for current borrowers to move to another plan. Borrowers who do not choose may be placed in a plan by the Department.
- **IBR.** Income-Based Repayment remains available to existing borrowers, which makes it an important option for people leaving other plans.
- **Standard repayment.** New loans made after July 1, 2026 are expected to have a standard plan with a term that varies by balance, as well as RAP.

Check which plan your servicer shows today, then compare it with what you will be eligible for. Moving plans can change both your monthly bill and the number of years until forgiveness.

## New borrowing limits

For new loans disbursed on or after July 1, 2026, the main limits are:

| Borrower type | Annual limit | Aggregate limit |
|---|---|---|
| Graduate students | $20,500 | $100,000 |
| Professional students (such as law or medicine) | $50,000 | $200,000 |
| Parent PLUS (per student) | $20,000 | $65,000 |

There is also a lifetime cap of $257,500 on federal borrowing per person (excluding Parent PLUS loans). Grad PLUS loans are no longer available to new borrowers. Students already enrolled and borrowing before the cutoff may have a transition period of a few years, so check how your own situation is treated.

Students who need more than the caps allow may turn to private loans, which usually lack income-driven repayment, forgiveness options or the same hardship protections. That trade-off is worth weighing before you borrow.

## Forgiveness paths

- **Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF).** PSLF remains in place for borrowers working for qualifying government and nonprofit employers, generally after 120 qualifying payments. Payments under RAP are expected to count. Keep your employer certification up to date.
- **Income-driven forgiveness.** Balances remaining after the plan's term (20 to 30 years depending on plan) may be forgiven. Starting in 2026, forgiven amounts under these plans are generally treated as taxable income again at the federal level, unless an exception applies. Plan for that possibility rather than assuming the balance simply disappears.
- **Discharges.** Total and permanent disability discharges and certain others remain available, with their own rules.

## Who is most affected

- **Recent graduates** entering repayment for the first time and choosing between RAP and a standard schedule.
- **Borrowers in SAVE** who have been in forbearance and now need a new plan.
- **Graduate and professional students** planning how to pay for programs under the new caps.
- **Parents** borrowing through Parent PLUS, who face new yearly and total limits.
- **Households with several dependents**, where the per-child payment reduction may matter.

## What to check on your servicer account

A short checklist you can do in about 20 minutes:

1. **Log in at StudentAid.gov** and confirm your loan types, balances and interest rates.
2. **Identify your current repayment plan** and whether your servicer says it is changing.
3. **Check your contact details.** Notices about plan changes often go out by email, and missed messages are a common cause of unexpected bills.
4. **Run the Loan Simulator** to compare your estimated monthly payment under each plan available to you.
5. **Review your income certification date.** Income-driven plans require annual recertification, and a late filing can raise your payment.
6. **Confirm your due date and autopay.** A plan change can reset the bill date and may affect an autopay discount.
7. **Look at your PSLF count**, if applicable, in the employment certification tool.
8. **Save records.** Keep screenshots or downloads of balances, payment counts and correspondence.

If anything looks wrong, contact your servicer in writing and keep a copy.

## Ripple effects on household budgets

A different monthly payment affects more than the loan itself.

- **Cash flow.** A lower payment can free up money for rent, childcare or emergency savings. A higher one may force tradeoffs elsewhere.
- **Predictability.** Income-based bills move as your AGI changes, which makes budgeting less steady for people with variable pay. Building a small buffer helps.
- **Interest and balance.** Paying less than the accrued interest can cause balances to grow under some plans. RAP's interest waiver and principal match are designed to limit that, but compare the numbers.
- **Big purchases.** Lenders look at debt-to-income ratio. A payment that rises or falls can change how much mortgage or auto loan you qualify for.
- **Taxes.** Any future taxable forgiveness is a reason to model long-term costs, not only next month's bill.

## Credit implications

Federal student loans are reported to credit bureaus, so repayment behavior matters.

- **On-time payments** help your history. Switching plans does not by itself hurt your credit when payments are made as billed.
- **Missed payments** can be reported after they are 90 days past due, and a default carries serious consequences, including collection actions such as wage garnishment and offset of tax refunds, which have resumed after the pandemic pause.
- **Forbearance and deferment** generally do not appear as late payments, but interest may continue to build.
- **Transition periods** are risky. If you move between plans and your servicer is slow, confirm the new amount and due date before the first bill is due.

If you cannot afford your payment, contact your servicer before you miss one. Options such as a lower-payment plan, a deferment or forbearance may be available.

## Planning tips

- Compare plans using total cost over time, not only the first year's bill.
- Recertify income on time every year.
- Beware of companies that charge fees for help you can get free from your servicer or StudentAid.gov.
- If you are still in school, borrow only what you need and learn the caps for your program.
- Revisit your plan when your income, family size or employer changes.

## Bottom line

The student loan reset gives some borrowers lower, more predictable payments and gives others a reason to re-run the numbers. The most useful thing you can do now is look at your own account, understand which plan you are on and how long it will be available, and compare the options before a deadline decides for you. Because the rules are still being implemented, rely on official sources for current details.

*This article is for general information only and does not constitute financial, tax or legal advice.*
